topic: the concept of genetic dominance and recessive alleles

easy.text: If an allele is 'dominant,' what does that mean?

options.text: Its trait will be expressed even if only one copy of that allele is present
options.feedback: Correct -- a dominant allele masks the effect of a recessive allele when paired together (heterozygous).

options.text: It is always the more common allele in a population
options.feedback: Dominance refers to how an allele's trait is expressed in a heterozygous pairing, not its frequency in the overall population.

options.text: It can only be expressed if two copies are present
options.feedback: That describes a RECESSIVE allele, not a dominant one -- dominant alleles are expressed even with just one copy.

options.text: It causes a genetic disease every time
options.feedback: Dominant alleles aren't necessarily harmful or disease-causing -- dominance simply refers to expression pattern, not health effect.

medium.text: In pea plants, purple flower color (P) is dominant over white flower color (p). A plant with genotype Pp (heterozygous) will have which flower color?

options.text: Purple, since the dominant P allele masks the recessive p allele
options.feedback: Correct -- with one dominant and one recessive allele, the dominant trait (purple) is what's visibly expressed.

options.text: White, since the recessive allele is still present
options.feedback: The mere presence of a recessive allele doesn't cause its trait to show -- with a dominant allele also present, the dominant trait (purple) is expressed instead.

options.text: A blend of purple and white, like light purple
options.feedback: Classic Mendelian dominance doesn't produce a blended color -- the dominant allele's trait (purple) is fully expressed, not mixed with the recessive trait.

options.text: It's impossible to predict the flower color from this genotype
options.feedback: This genotype's phenotype is actually quite predictable using standard dominance rules -- Pp results in purple flowers.

hard.text: Two heterozygous (Pp) pea plants are crossed. Using a Punnett square, what fraction of their offspring would be expected to have white flowers (genotype pp)?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Punnett square for Pp × Pp gives genotype ratios of 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp, meaning 1 out of 4 offspring (25%) would be pp (white).
This doesn't match the actual Punnett square outcome for a Pp × Pp cross, which gives a 1:2:1 genotype ratio, with only 1/4 being pp.
This is actually the fraction expected to show the PURPLE phenotype (PP + Pp combined), not the white (pp) phenotype.

options.text: 0% -- no offspring could have white flowers
options.feedback: Since both parents carry a recessive p allele, there IS a nonzero chance of pp offspring appearing -- specifically 1/4 of the offspring.

easy.hard: This describes an allele whose associated trait manifests phenotypically even in a heterozygous genetic combination.
easy.medium: This kind of allele shows up in the organism's traits even if there's only one copy of it.
easy.easy: This kind of allele shows up even with just one copy of it.

medium.hard: Determine which allele's trait is visibly expressed when one dominant and one recessive allele are both present together.
medium.medium: With one dominant (P) and one recessive (p) allele together, which trait actually shows up?
medium.easy: With one purple allele and one white allele together, purple wins since it's dominant.

hard.hard: Construct a 2x2 Punnett square crossing Pp with Pp, then count how many of the four resulting genotype combinations are homozygous recessive.
hard.medium: Draw out all four possible combinations of P and p from each parent, then count how many end up as pp.
hard.easy: Out of the 4 possible combinations (PP, Pp, Pp, pp), only 1 is pp -- that's 1 out of 4.
